title: Key diagram
instance: The sub-diagrams below are this drawing with the lanes renamed and the slots filled. Nothing in the protocol touches the Principal or Buyer lanes; the Agent is the x402 client.
lanes: the person or org the purchase is for
the person who runs the agent
slots: Who delegated what to whom, and when. Three things that are easy to blur (Nicole, Oct 27 00:32–00:36): identity answers “who is this?”; delegation is the scope the agent got (which sellers, what budget, what time window, what permissions); the audit trail ties both to one transaction so the chain can be rebuilt later. Limits are a separate note (Alfred [00:37:59], Nicole [00:38:01] “Check.”); whether delegated authority is in scope waits on the TSC.
The seller’s disclosure profile, and what comes back

B is the region between M1 and M4. The seller’s requirement is not a universal minimum: each seller sets two dials (Nicole, Oct 27 00:37–00:42): which fields it needs (email, org ID, human ID) and what assurance each needs (self-attested, or verified by a third party). The assurance steps up with the value or kind of transaction (Reuben, Oct 27 00:42). The 402 is the ask and M3 is the answer; the spec has no separate identity message (Krystal [00:32:51], Nicole [00:34:00]).
The wallet address is the identifier anchor

The payload proves control of the paying wallet and nothing more. A wallet is an account, an identifier; it is not an identity, which is a legal person or an organization (Adrian, Oct 27; accepted by Alfred). The anchor is the stable identifier the evidence chain hangs on (Nicole [00:51:53]); linking it to an identity is the separate dashed step below it (RFP 4.2.1).
The fields the seller needs and the assurance level it needs for each, set from its own risk tolerance and logged as evidence (Nicole [00:47:38], Krystal [00:50:34]).

Audit, dispute and limit evidence. A Verifier checks the record and a Relying Party acts on it; neither sends or receives a protocol message, so they are not lanes (RFP 1.2 actors). Signed offers and receipts are the nearest protocol extension. Limit evidence is still open (Nicole [00:30:16]).
footer: x402 v2 names three parties (client, resource server, facilitator) and identifies a payer only by wallet address. The signature on the payload proves control of that wallet for one transfer, nothing about who stands behind it.

Placements, not designs: A at delegation, B the region where the seller states its profile and the buyer answers, C in the payload, with the identity link a separate step. The protocol’s own extensions field is where B and C ride.
K0 assumes none. Each sub-diagram states the tier its case assumes: self-attested, provable, or issued by an authority.

Mechanism for every slot · whether x402 should recommend a universal minimum profile (Nicole, Oct 27: a requirement, perhaps, not the drawing) · whether M4/M5 is where an external-identity authorization sits (Joseph, Oct 27; Alfred: too prescriptive for requirements) · whether delegated authority and limits are in scope (TSC) · whether the wallet signature is enough (T7) · who holds the developer-to-org mapping (T5) · what, if anything, is recorded after settlement.
